ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All procedures were approved by the Research Ethics Board at the University of Toronto (protocol 41533), and the study was carried out in accordance with all relevant regulations regarding human-participants research.
The study was approved by the University of Toronto's Research Ethics Board (Protocol 41533)

To preview our results, we see improved spatial accuracy across our gaze-contingent video termination conditions, with the most accurate localization when participants are able to fixate the video, the worst performance when they are reliant on covert attention alone and intermediate performance when only presaccadic information is available.

Per our preregistration (https://osf.io/u3str), 34 licensed drivers from the University of Toronto Mississauga undergraduate research participant pool (aged 18-35; mean age = 19.794 years; 22 female, 12 male; 23 G2 or equivalent, 11 G or equivalent) were included in the final sample.

table.text: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision with near acuities of 20/25 or better, based on assessment with the near ETDRS test at 40 cm viewing distance.

table.text: Together, these factors manipulated when within the video participants were instructed to move their eyes toward the video and how much visual information was available after they were told to do so.
Participants were instructed to move their eyes from the fixation point to the video as quickly and as accurately as possible as soon as they heard the cue.

This criterion served to terminate the video after participants had initiated a saccade toward the cued video, but before they obtained foveal information from the target region, thereby isolating presaccadic visual input and its processing.
Participants were required to have a maximum eye tracking error below 1.5º for all calibration locations to be eligible to complete the study.
table.header: Gaze-contingent termination implementation and gaze data quality

table.text: At the start of each trial, participants were required to fixate a 0.5° x 0.5° (24px x 24px) green fixation square 10.72° below video center.
Participants were instructed to maintain fixation on the fixation square until an auditory cue, where they should look towards the video.
Participants were told that if fixation was not maintained, the trial would not be valid.
Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible.

All participants were shown all 216 hazard present videos in randomized order and with random assignment on a videowise basis in the cue onset and gaze-contingent termination conditions such that each participant completed an equal number of trials for each unique combination of conditions.

Prior to the main experimental blocks, participants were required to successfully complete a practice to learn the task by achieving 80% valid trials in a 10-trials block (that is, making a timely saccade when cued on 8 of 10 practice trials in the block).
Participants were given the chance to ask questions after the practice.
Participants were also encouraged to take a break halfway through the experiment.
After completing the experiment, participants were asked to complete a driving history questionnaire.
The experiment took approximately one hour and 20 minutes, and participants were compensated $20 CAD for their time.

All participants provided informed consent prior to participating.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 8 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: As seen in Figure 2, the model error differed significantly from zero, (F(1, 33) = 995.45, p < 0.0001), indicating click errors were significantly lower than under the permuted null distribution.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: The ANOVA also revealed a significant main effect of cue timing, (F(2, 66) = 23.598, p < 0.0001), such that localization improved as the auditory cue was presented closer to hazard onset.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: There was a significant main effect of gaze-contingent video termination condition, (F(2, 66) = 9.398, p < 0.001) suggesting attentional resources were, as expected from the literature with static images and stimuli, presaccadically allocated towards the target object, as shown by improved localization precision.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: However, there was no significant interaction between cue timing and gaze-contingent video termination condition, (F(4, 132) = 1.163, p = 0.33), indicating that this effect of saccadic attentional shifts was related to when participants made saccades, rather than when the hazard became dangerous in the stimulus videos.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: Figure 3 participants' saccade landing error decreased with cue time (F(2,66) = 15.31, p < 0.0001), such that the closer the cue was to hazard onset, the more they looked towards the hazard compared to the null distribution of saccade landings.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: Additionally, there was a significant main effect of gaze-contingent video termination condition (F(2, 66) = 4.243, p= 0.0185), however, there was no interaction between the conditions (F(4, 132) = 1.132, p = 0.3445), suggesting that differences in accuracy of reported hazard position were driven by better saccade planning across some of the termination conditions.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: Additionally, there was a significant main effect of gaze-contingent video termination condition (F(2, 66) = 4.243, p= 0.0185), however, there was no interaction between the conditions (F(4, 132) = 1.132, p = 0.3445), suggesting that differences in accuracy of reported hazard position were driven by better saccade planning across some of the termination conditions.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: As shown in Figure 3, a repeated measures ANOVA on z-scores across both unique conditions differed significantly from zero (F(1,33) = 892.24, p<0.0001), suggesting that participants used scene information to look towards the hazard.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 30 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: To preview our results, we see improved spatial accuracy across our gaze-contingent video termination conditions, with the most accurate localization when participants are able to fixate the video, the worst performance when they are reliant on covert attention alone and intermediate performance when only presaccadic information is available.

Per our preregistration (https://osf.io/u3str), 34 licensed drivers from the University of Toronto Mississauga undergraduate research participant pool (aged 18-35; mean age = 19.794 years; 22 female, 12 male; 23 G2 or equivalent, 11 G or equivalent) were included in the final sample.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision with near acuities of 20/25 or better, based on assessment with the near ETDRS test at 40 cm viewing distance.
Four participants were replaced in accordance with our preregistered data quality checks.
Participants provided informed consent before participating in the study.
Participants were instructed to shift gaze to the video immediately at the auditory cue.
Videos were followed by a 250ms mask, after which participants were prompted to report hazard position at video termination using a cursor, within a black rectangle at the position of video.
Together, these factors manipulated when within the video participants were instructed to move their eyes toward the video and how much visual information was available after they were told to do so.
Participants were instructed to move their eyes from the fixation point to the video as quickly and as accurately as possible as soon as they heard the cue.

This criterion served to terminate the video after participants had initiated a saccade toward the cued video, but before they obtained foveal information from the target region, thereby isolating presaccadic visual input and its processing.
Participants were required to have a maximum eye tracking error below 1.5º for all calibration locations to be eligible to complete the study.
At the start of each trial, participants were required to fixate a 0.5° x 0.5° (24px x 24px) green fixation square 10.72° below video center.
Participants were instructed to maintain fixation on the fixation square until an auditory cue, where they should look towards the video.
Participants were told that if fixation was not maintained, the trial would not be valid.
Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible.

All participants were shown all 216 hazard present videos in randomized order and with random assignment on a videowise basis in the cue onset and gaze-contingent termination conditions such that each participant completed an equal number of trials for each unique combination of conditions.

Prior to the main experimental blocks, participants were required to successfully complete a practice to learn the task by achieving 80% valid trials in a 10-trials block (that is, making a timely saccade when cued on 8 of 10 practice trials in the block).
Participants were given the chance to ask questions after the practice.
Participants were also encouraged to take a break halfway through the experiment.
After completing the experiment, participants were asked to complete a driving history questionnaire.
The experiment took approximately one hour and 20 minutes, and participants were compensated $20 CAD for their time.

Each line represents a different gaze-contingent termination as labeled in the To determine whether hazard localization was better than expected if participants were not using video-specific scene information, and whether this effect differed across conditions, we analyzed click-error z-scores using a 3x3 repeated-measures ANOVA with cue timing and gazecontingent termination as within-participant factors.
All participants provided informed consent prior to participating.

info.title: Presaccadic Attention in Dynamic Scenes: Evidence from Hazard Localization in Road Videos

text.text: Presaccadic shifts of attention immediately prior to the movement of the eye have been extensively reported since the 1990s.
However, all of these studies have used static images, often isolated objects on a neutral background, which do not much resemble the world we inhabit.

Here, we use videos of rapidly-evolving road scenes to examine whether presaccadic attention operates in a similar manner when the observer needs to plan a speeded saccade to a target embedded within a complex, changing scene.

Using a gaze-contingent paradigm, we isolated covert attention, presaccadic attention and overt attention, as well as manipulating the relative informativeness of the scene by varying the time at which the observer initiated their saccade.

We find progressive improvements in localisation performance across our covert attention, presaccadic attention and overt attention conditions, but do not find evidence that the increasing informativeness of the scene over time modulates these effects, pointing to presaccadic attention as inherent to saccade planning and execution.

This work represents a first step in extending our understanding of saccade planning processes to dynamic scenes, and lays the groundwork for future studies of what information is acquired prior to a saccade in daily life.
Attentional shifts prior to saccadic eye movements are an essential component of saccade planning and our perception of a stable visual world.

Presaccadic shifts of attention have been shown to improve perception of object form (Deubel & Schneider, 1996; Kwak et al., 2023) and the precision of the subsequent eye movements (Zhao et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Presaccadic shifts of attention have been shown to improve perception of object form <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Deubel & Schneider, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Kwak et al., 2023)</ref> and the precision of the subsequent eye movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Zhao et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These results may be (and likely are) linked to the phenomenon of saccadic remapping, but presaccadic shifts of attention have been shown to be a separate process, drawing on independent attentional resources (c.f., Rolfs et al., 2010).
text.formatted: These results may be (and likely are) linked to the phenomenon of saccadic remapping, but presaccadic shifts of attention have been shown to be a separate process, drawing on independent attentional resources (c.f., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Rolfs et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As attentional resources are limited, their precise and accurate direction is needed for effective exploration of the visual world and localization of potential saccade targets (as discussed in Kowler et al., 1995 and Rolfs, 2015).
text.formatted: As attentional resources are limited, their precise and accurate direction is needed for effective exploration of the visual world and localization of potential saccade targets (as discussed in <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Kowler et al., 1995 and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Rolfs, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A presaccadic shift of attention appears to increase the fidelity of representations prior to the saccade, which are then further enhanced after the eye lands on or near the target (Zhao et al., 2012).
text.formatted: A presaccadic shift of attention appears to increase the fidelity of representations prior to the saccade, which are then further enhanced after the eye lands on or near the target <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Zhao et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These effects are well established, but have previously been studied with simple visual tasks, often with one isolated target, or, at most, a handful of isolated, static objects on a screen.

As the world outside the laboratory is neither that empty nor that motionless, it remains unclear whether presaccadic attention operates in the same way in dynamic and complex scenes like those we encounter in our daily lives.
Using videos of road scenes as an example of complex, crowded and time-limited scenes, we aim to determine whether presaccadic attention operates similarly in this context.
Presaccadic attention is a deployment of attention towards the target of the impending saccade and occurs gradually in the 50-150ms prior to the observable start of a saccade (Deubel, 2008).
text.formatted: Presaccadic attention is a deployment of attention towards the target of the impending saccade and occurs gradually in the 50-150ms prior to the observable start of a saccade <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Deubel, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: This attentional deployment is necessary for saccadic guidance (Kowler et al., 1995) and increases visual acuity at the target location (Kwak et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This attentional deployment is necessary for saccadic guidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Kowler et al., 1995)</ref> and increases visual acuity at the target location <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Kwak et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These perceptual benefits at the target location improve performance at both the feature (Li et al., 2019) and object level (Wolfe & Whitney, 2014), as well as reducing crowding and improving spatial localization (Greenwood et al., 2017).
text.formatted: These perceptual benefits at the target location improve performance at both the feature <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Li et al., 2019)</ref> and object level <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Wolfe & Whitney, 2014)</ref>, as well as reducing crowding and improving spatial localization <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Greenwood et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, these presaccadic improvements do not rise to the level of post-saccadic (foveal) information (Rolfs, 2015), but provide a measurable difference in performance that sits between what is achievable by the observer with covert attention and what they can achieve when foveating the target object (Kwak et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Notably, these presaccadic improvements do not rise to the level of post-saccadic (foveal) information <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Rolfs, 2015)</ref>, but provide a measurable difference in performance that sits between what is achievable by the observer with covert attention and what they can achieve when foveating the target object <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Kwak et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Reflecting this, we separate our consideration of attentional shifts towards a peripheral target into covert attention (> 150ms prior to saccade onset); presaccadic attention (150-50ms prior to saccade onset) and overt attention (> 100ms after saccade landing on/near target).
text.formatted: Reflecting this, we separate our consideration of attentional shifts towards a peripheral target into covert attention (> 150ms prior to saccade onset); presaccadic attention (150-50ms prior to saccade onset) and overt attention (> 100ms after saccade landing on/near target).

text.text: If presaccadic attention is, in fact, an integral part of saccade planning and an element of how the visual system achieves visual stability in spite of eye movements, it should operate similarly in dynamic scenes.
However, the prior work which has characterized presaccadic attention has been done with single isolated objects or a small handful of objects, exclusively in static stimulus arrays.

Environments outside the lab are, of course, cluttered and dynamic, with a great deal of information that the observer must contend with to plan their saccades, to say nothing of the tendency of objects in the world to move (as well as the active observer's own behaviour moving through the environment).
In this work, we used an existing set of dashcam videos containing near-collision scenes, since these scenes are both complex and rapidly evolving (Song et al., 2023; Song et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In this work, we used an existing set of dashcam videos containing near-collision scenes, since these scenes are both complex and rapidly evolving <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Song et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Song et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These scenes are far more complex than stimuli which have been previously used in the study of presaccadic attention (c.f., Song et al., 2023) and contain a range of relevant and irrelevant information at different locations in frame (Wolfe et al., 2020).
text.formatted: These scenes are far more complex than stimuli which have been previously used in the study of presaccadic attention (c.f., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Song et al., 2023)</ref> and contain a range of relevant and irrelevant information at different locations in frame <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Wolfe et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These scenes are particularly useful, as hazards, which may result in collisions or near-collisions, have some statistical regularities and evolve over time (Song et al., 2026), and one can think of the scene becoming more informative relative to the hazard as the situation evolves.
text.formatted: These scenes are particularly useful, as hazards, which may result in collisions or near-collisions, have some statistical regularities and evolve over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Song et al., 2026)</ref>, and one can think of the scene becoming more informative relative to the hazard as the situation evolves.

text.text: That is, it should become clearer to the observer that this car (or pedestrian, or moose) is worth attending to, and making an eye movement towards, because it might be relevant to the larger task of avoiding a collision.

The dense and rapid nature of these videos makes them a particularly useful way to examine presaccadic attention in a more naturalistic manner, rather than out of any inherent focus on driving and driver behaviour.

If presaccadic attentional shifts prior to saccadic eye movements are useful in real-world dynamic scenes, we would expect to observe similar separation across the three eye-movement conditions of covert, presaccadic, and overt attention, to those found in previous presaccadic object localization studies (He & Kowler, 1991; Vishwanath & Kowler, 2003), such that spatial accuracy increases as the eye movement unfolds and more attentional resources are directed towards the targeted location before the eye physically begins to move.
text.formatted: If presaccadic attentional shifts prior to saccadic eye movements are useful in real-world dynamic scenes, we would expect to observe similar separation across the three eye-movement conditions of covert, presaccadic, and overt attention, to those found in previous presaccadic object localization studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(He & Kowler, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Vishwanath & Kowler, 2003)</ref>, such that spatial accuracy increases as the eye movement unfolds and more attentional resources are directed towards the targeted location before the eye physically begins to move.

text.text: Conversely, if presaccadic attentional shifts are not informative under these conditions, we would expect no change across our three conditions.

We also posit that participants may be able to use the larger structure of the scene to better plan their saccades, and that if they are able to use this global information, we would expect an interaction between the informativeness of the scene (the auditory cue time conditions) and the gaze-contingent video termination conditions.

To preview our results, we see improved spatial accuracy across our gaze-contingent video termination conditions, with the most accurate localization when participants are able to fixate the video, the worst performance when they are reliant on covert attention alone and intermediate performance when only presaccadic information is available.

A red rectangle is superimposed here to highlight the location of the hazard at each of the three timepoints for the auditory cue, but were not present in the study.

The video was terminated based on a gaze-contingent termination condition as described in the figure, either at the onset of the auditory cue (Covert Attention), once the saccade towards the video had begun (Pre-Saccadic Attention), or 100ms after gaze entered the region of the screen where the video was presented (Overt Attention).
Videos were followed by a 250ms mask, after which participants were prompted to report hazard position at video termination using a cursor, within a black rectangle at the position of video.
Videos in the main experimental blocks all contained hazards, examples of which are seen in figure (B) with a red rectangle around hazard objects.
Video stimuli were forward-facing dashcam footage of real road scenes from the Road Hazard Stimuli dataset (Song et al., 2023; Wolfe et al., 2020).

text.text: All videos in the experimental condition contained hazards, which are defined as objects on the road that require an immediate response by a driver to avoid a collision.

Hazards varied in type (other vehicles, pedestrians, cyclists, animals), location of appearance (adjacent lanes, lane of travel, adjacent to roadway), and scene environment (urban, suburban, highway, rural).
The timing and location of each hazard from hazard onset and later were annotated by two independent annotators and verified by a third for agreement (Song et al., 2023).

text.text: Practice videos were also sourced from the Road Hazard Stimuli, but did not contain hazards.

The size of the maximum display area was 54.5º by 32.3º, at a viewing distance of 57cm maintained with a chinrest.

text.text: Together, these factors manipulated when within the video participants were instructed to move their eyes toward the video and how much visual information was available after they were told to do so.
During each trial, an auditory cue (15ms, 44khz) to initiate a saccade was provided at one of three time points: 1.5s pre-hazard onset, 0.5s pre-hazard onset, or at hazard onset.
Participants were instructed to move their eyes from the fixation point to the video as quickly and as accurately as possible as soon as they heard the cue.
Following the auditory cue, videos were terminated according to one of three gazecontingent termination levels.

These levels were designed to isolate increasingly later stages of visual processing during gaze shifts toward the video (in line with Kwak et al., 2023): covert attention, presaccadic attention, and overt attention (first fixation).
text.formatted: These levels were designed to isolate increasingly later stages of visual processing during gaze shifts toward the video (in line with <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Kwak et al., 2023)</ref>: covert attention, presaccadic attention, and overt attention (first fixation).

text.text: In the covert attention condition, the video terminated immediately at the onset of the auditory cue, such that video was terminated before any eye movement planning toward the video occurred.
In the presaccadic attention condition, the video was terminated once participants' gaze moved 1.49° (70 pixels) above the fixation point's upper edge.

This criterion served to terminate the video after participants had initiated a saccade toward the cued video, but before they obtained foveal information from the target region, thereby isolating presaccadic visual input and its processing.
Finally, in the overt attention condition, videos terminated 100ms after participants' gaze entered the video region.
This condition allowed participants to acquire initial fixational information from the video, while preventing additional gaze shifts (Nuthmann, 2016).
text.formatted: This condition allowed participants to acquire initial fixational information from the video, while preventing additional gaze shifts <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Nuthmann, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: On all trials, participants reported where they thought the hazardous object was at the time of video termination using the onscreen cursor and by controlling the mouse.
Responses were made on a black response rectangle that matched the position and dimensions of the video display.

A 9-point calibration (covering a 25.6° by 17.2° rectangle centered on screen center) was performed at the start of each of the two blocks, and whenever participants removed their chin from the chinrest.
Participants were required to have a maximum eye tracking error below 1.5º for all calibration locations to be eligible to complete the study.
Additionally, single-point screen-centre drift checks were performed every 25 trials.
For the two gaze-contingent video termination conditions, video termination was controlled online using real-time gaze position samples from the EyeLink 1000.
Gaze position was evaluated and the display was updated on each screen refresh, at a rate of 60 Hz.

Thus, termination for all conditions occurred at the screen refresh after the termination criterion was met, with minimal additional delay from rendering time and monitor refresh latency (Saunders & Woods, 2013).
text.formatted: Thus, termination for all conditions occurred at the screen refresh after the termination criterion was met, with minimal additional delay from rendering time and monitor refresh latency <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Saunders & Woods, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: At the start of each trial, participants were required to fixate a 0.5° x 0.5° (24px x 24px) green fixation square 10.72° below video center.
The trial began after gaze position was within 1.49° (70px) from fixation center for an uninterrupted 790ms.
The green fixation square turned black to indicate trial start, and after a 250ms noise mask, the video began.
Videos subtended 31.6° horizontally and 17.23° vertically (31.43 x 17.15 cm) at a viewing distance of 57 cm.
Participants were instructed to maintain fixation on the fixation square until an auditory cue, where they should look towards the video.
Participants were told that if fixation was not maintained, the trial would not be valid.
They were further instructed that the video would terminate close to the auditory cue and that an insufficiently quick saccade towards the video would also result in an invalid trial.

The auditory cue, which instructed participants to move their eyes, occurred at one of three time points relative to hazard onset as explained above (1500ms prior to hazard onset, 500ms prior to hazard onset, at hazard onset).
As an additional signal to move their eyes, the fixation square was removed when the auditory cue was presented.

Concurrently with this, the gaze-contingent termination procedure was triggered (covert attention [coterminal with auditory cue]; presaccadic attention [> 70px gaze shift away from fixation box location]; overt attention [100ms following gaze entrance into the video region]).
text.formatted: Concurrently with this, the gaze-contingent termination procedure was triggered (covert attention [coterminal with auditory cue]; presaccadic attention [> 70px gaze shift away from fixation box location]; overt attention [100ms following gaze entrance into the video region]).

text.text: Following video termination, a second noise mask with a duration of 250ms was shown, followed by a black rectangle at video position and dimensions with the cursor located at a randomized starting location within the rectangle.
Participants' task on all trials was to report hazard position at the moment of video termination by clicking the corresponding location in the black rectangle.
Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible.
If participants clicked outside the response rectangle they were prompted to respond within the rectangle.

All participants were shown all 216 hazard present videos in randomized order and with random assignment on a videowise basis in the cue onset and gaze-contingent termination conditions such that each participant completed an equal number of trials for each unique combination of conditions.

If a participant either failed to maintain fixation prior to the auditory cue or failed to make a saccade towards the video within 500ms of auditory cue presentation, they received immediate auditory feedback and visual feedback.
The video was immediately replaced by a red rectangle, and they heard a 500ms tone (400hz and 1200hz sinusoidal components sampled at 10khz).
The red rectangle and tone feedback indicated to the participant that the trial was invalid and was intended to reduce subsequent invalid trials.

Prior to the main experimental blocks, participants were required to successfully complete a practice to learn the task by achieving 80% valid trials in a 10-trials block (that is, making a timely saccade when cued on 8 of 10 practice trials in the block).

Videos within the practice blocks did not include a hazard event, but were similarly programed with auditory cues to teach participants to make a saccade at the same times as in the experimental trials.
Participants continued to complete practice blocks until they met this criterion or failed 9 practice blocks.
If they failed 9 practice blocks, they were excluded from the study.
Participants were given the chance to ask questions after the practice.
Participants were also encouraged to take a break halfway through the experiment.
After completing the experiment, participants were asked to complete a driving history questionnaire.
The experiment took approximately one hour and 20 minutes, and participants were compensated $20 CAD for their time.
Trials were excluded according to three eye-movement related criteria.
First, trials were excluded if participants moved their gaze more than 1.49° (70 pixels) above the center of the fixation square before the auditory cue.
This criterion ensured participants did not fixate the video before they received the cue to make a saccade, preventing multiple or premature fixations on the video.
Second, we excluded trials where participants failed to move gaze at least 1.49° above fixation square center within 500ms of the auditory cue.
This ensured participants initiated an eye-movement within the intended interval, limiting differences in time sensitive visual information across gaze-contingent video termination conditions.
Finally, trials were excluded if the first saccade they made did not land within the video region.
This criterion ensured included trials reflect eye movements towards the video region.
For each valid trial, hazard localization error was computed as the shortest Euclidean distance between the participant's mouse-click response and the annotated hazard position at hazard onset.
Hazard position was acquired from the Road Hazard Stimuli annotations (Song et al., 2023), and distances were computed using the p_poly_dist function (Yoshpe, 2025; MathWorks, 2025).
text.formatted: Hazard position was acquired from the Road Hazard Stimuli annotations <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Song et al., 2023)</ref>, and distances were computed using the p_poly_dist function <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Yoshpe, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">MathWorks, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Clicks falling within the hazard polygon were assigned an error of 0.
For each participant, mean click error was then calculated across all valid trials.
Gaze error was calculated using a comparable procedure.

For each valid trial, we computed the shortest Euclidean distance between first post-cue fixation within the video region and the annotated hazard position at hazard onset, again using p_poly_dist (Yoshpe, 2025; MathWorks, 2025).

text.text: Mean gaze error was then calculated for each participant across all valid trials.

As videos per unique condition differed between participants, and because annotated hazard position and size at hazard onset varied substantially across videos (Song et al., 2023), raw error may reflect video level differences rather than condition level differences.

text.text: We therefore transformed raw errors into participant-specific and unique level-specific across both conditions z-scores relative to a permuted null distribution (Hesterberg et al., 2003).

text.text: This approach estimated whether participants' results were closer to hazard location than would be expected if their responses did not include video-specific scene information.
Null distributions were calculated separately for each participant and each unique condition.

For click error, the null distribution was computed by randomly shuffling mapping between click location and annotated hazard location to randomly reassign the video identity associated with each click position within each participant and unique condition for 5000 iterations.
For each iteration, we calculated the mean click-to-hazard distance, producing a null distribution of errors expected under click behavior devoid of video level information (Figure 1B).

text.text: Results were then converted to a Z-score using Z = 𝜇 𝑅𝑎𝑤 -𝜇 𝑁𝑢𝑙𝑙 𝜎 𝑁𝑢𝑙𝑙 , for each participant and unique condition.
The same procedure was applied to gaze error, except that first-fixation locations were shuffled instead of click locations.

To examine whether participants' use of scene information differed across auditory cue timing and gaze-contingent video termination conditions, we conducted a 3x3 within-participants categorical ANOVA on hazard-localization z-scores including an interaction between the conditions.
We then conducted paired-samples t-tests comparing all pairs for each significant main effect condition.
To control for the influence of saccade latency on click error, we fitted two Generalized Linear Mixed Effects Models (LMEs) on condition level data.

Models included per participant mean Z-score for each unique condition as a dependent variable, with gaze-contingent video termination condition and auditory cue timing condition as categorical variables (both LMEs included mean saccade latency after the cue as an independent variable) and participant number as a random variable.
The difference between both LMEs was that one included an interaction between gaze-contingent video termination condition and saccade latency, while the other did not.

As both did not show significant main effects or interactions for saccade latency, results for these analyses are included in the Supplementary Materials. participant included, on average, 19.529 valid trials, with a minimum of 11 valid trials.

As seen in Figure 2, the model error differed significantly from zero, (F(1, 33) = 995.45, p < 0.0001), indicating click errors were significantly lower than under the permuted null distribution.

text.text: This suggests that, across conditions, participants used scene information to localize the hazard, resulting in better hazard localization performance.
The ANOVA also revealed a significant main effect of cue timing, (F(2, 66) = 23.598, p < 0.0001), such that localization improved as the auditory cue was presented closer to hazard onset.
text.formatted: The ANOVA also revealed a significant main effect of cue timing, (F(2, 66) = 23.598, p < 0.0001), such that localization improved as the auditory cue was presented closer to hazard onset.

text.text: This pattern is consistent with the fact that later cue times provide participants with more task-relevant information by showing video closer to hazard onset, as hazards evolve and become more distinct and recognizable to observers over time.
Following the significant main effect of cue timing, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons were conducted.

Z-scores differed significantly between all times such that the closer cue timing is to hazard onset, the more precise the localization was compared to a permuted null (full table of pairwise comparisons in Supplementary Materials).
Overall, these results suggest that as the scene unfolds, more task relevant information is present for observers to use for more accurate localization of hazards.

There was a significant main effect of gaze-contingent video termination condition, (F(2, 66) = 9.398, p < 0.001) suggesting attentional resources were, as expected from the literature with static images and stimuli, presaccadically allocated towards the target object, as shown by improved localization precision.

text.text: However, there was no significant interaction between cue timing and gaze-contingent video termination condition, (F(4, 132) = 1.163, p = 0.33), indicating that this effect of saccadic attentional shifts was related to when participants made saccades, rather than when the hazard became dangerous in the stimulus videos.
Following the significant main effect of the gaze-contingent video termination condition, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons were conducted.

Z-scores differed significantly between covert attention and overt attention conditions (Mdiff = 0.63, SE = 0.15, 95% CI = [0.25, 1.01], p <0.0001), such that participants more accurately localized hazards if they were able to fixate the target of their saccade before the video was removed from the screen, compared to covert attention alone.

text.text: The difference between the covert attention condition and presaccadic attention condition was not significant (Mdiff = 0.27, SE = 0.13, 95% CI = [-0.06, 0.60], p = .139), nor was the difference between presaccadic attention and overt attention (Mdiff = 0.36, SE = 0.16, 95% CI = [-0.04, 0.77], p = .09), suggesting localization accuracy using presaccadic attention is somewhere between covert attention and overt attention.

Overall, results from the Z-scored click errors suggest an improvement in accuracy with additional hazard relevant scene information as well as eye movement information, in line with a presaccadic attention account.

text.text: Additionally, there was a significant main effect of gaze-contingent video termination condition (F(2, 66) = 4.243, p= 0.0185), however, there was no interaction between the conditions (F(4, 132) = 1.132, p = 0.3445), suggesting that differences in accuracy of reported hazard position were driven by better saccade planning across some of the termination conditions.

To identify differences between levels in the gaze-contingent video termination condition, pairwise comparisons with a Bonferroni correction (critical alpha = 0.0167) were performed for all unique comparisons in the termination condition.

Pairwise comparison between presaccadic attention and covert attention Z-scores showed a significant difference between the conditions (Mdiff = 0.462, SE = 0.155, 95% CI = [0.070 0.853], p = 0.0164), suggesting presaccadic attention supported more accurate saccades compared to covert attention alone.

Conversely, comparison between overt attention and covert attention Z-scores showed no significant difference between the conditions (Mdiff = 0.166, SE = 0.137, 95% CI = [-0.1803, 0.5114], p=0.7077); similarly, no significant difference was found between overt attention and presaccadic attention conditions (Mdiff = 0.296, SE = 0.18, 95% CI = [-0.748, 0.156], p = 0.3252).
Overall, the overt attention z-score results suggest that later cue timing not only improved observers' explicit reports of hazard location but also improved initial gaze guidance toward the hazards.
Additionally, differences in landing error between gaze-contingent video termination conditions support an account of presaccadic attention's role in helping direct saccadic eye movements.

Here, we aimed to address a gap in the literature concerning whether presaccadic attention, which had been previously reported only in experiments which used static, isolated, stimuli, could be observed in dynamic stimuli which more closely resembled real-world environments.

Using a video-based gaze-contingent paradigm, we demonstrated that, similar to previous work with static images, observers are better able to localize target objects if they have begun to plan a saccade, but that that this improvement, which we argue is a presaccadic shift of attention, does not bring task performance to the level achieved by fixating the target.

While previous research has shown information acquired during presaccadic attentional shifts can be used outside of basic feature discrimination, and provides object selective input (Wolfe & Whitney, 2015; He & Kowler, 1991; Vishwanath & Kowler, 2003), such that it may allow for object-form information within scenes (Castelhano & Pereira, 2018), these studies did not explore complex naturalistic stimuli, much less moving naturalistic stimuli.
text.formatted: While previous research has shown information acquired during presaccadic attentional shifts can be used outside of basic feature discrimination, and provides object selective input <ref type="bibr">(Wolfe & Whitney, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">He & Kowler, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Vishwanath & Kowler, 2003)</ref>, such that it may allow for object-form information within scenes <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Castelhano & Pereira, 2018)</ref>, these studies did not explore complex naturalistic stimuli, much less moving naturalistic stimuli.

text.text: Using our gazecontingent video termination paradigm, with a hazard localization task, we demonstrated that information gathered during presaccadic attention is task informative to a degree between covert attention (peripheral vision) and overt attention (first fixation) regardless of saccade latency, aligning with this previous work with static images.
Our findings support an account of presaccadic attention serving localization functions prior to fixation.
Notably, this role of presaccadic information was not linked to changes in how much task-relevant information was available in the scene prior to and during saccade planning.

At least in our task, additional attentional resources allocated during a saccadic eye movement increased precision in hazard localization, but this was not dependent on whether the hazard itself had become obvious in the video, pointing to a tightly bounded temporal effect linked to the saccade itself.

As previously described, presaccadic attention is operative in a narrow window immediately prior to the saccade itself (beginning, at most, 150ms prior), and our results suggest that information prior to this short presaccadic window is not a substantial factor.

However, our method only probed spatial precision, and future work in dynamic scenes could investigate whether presaccadic attention improves representational detail (as previously reported with isolated or crowded objects; e.g., Wolfe and Whitney 2014).

Our results are in line with the limited static scene literature on presaccadic attention (Castelhano & Pereira, 2018) which showed no interaction between scene-object context consistency and improved object processing at presaccadic object preview.
text.formatted: Our results are in line with the limited static scene literature on presaccadic attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Castelhano & Pereira, 2018)</ref> which showed no interaction between scene-object context consistency and improved object processing at presaccadic object preview.

text.text: More recent work on how feature level and object level processing progresses as the eye movement unfolds suggests presaccadic attention improves visual acuity (Kwak et al., 2023).
text.formatted: More recent work on how feature level and object level processing progresses as the eye movement unfolds suggests presaccadic attention improves visual acuity <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Kwak et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This work builds on prior work with the aforementioned static images demonstrating that presaccadic attention improves spatial precision (Vishwanath & Kowler, 2003) and reduces crowding (Wolfe & Whitney, 2014) at the location of an impending saccade prior to the eye movement.
text.formatted: This work builds on prior work with the aforementioned static images demonstrating that presaccadic attention improves spatial precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Vishwanath & Kowler, 2003)</ref> and reduces crowding <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Wolfe & Whitney, 2014)</ref> at the location of an impending saccade prior to the eye movement.

text.text: It is likely that all of these effects are part and parcel of the benefits of presaccadic shifts of attention, and that these effects are likely quite spatially specific around the saccade target (Greenwood et al., 2017), rather than representing an increase in attention to the entire scene (Castelhano & Pereira, 2018).
text.formatted: It is likely that all of these effects are part and parcel of the benefits of presaccadic shifts of attention, and that these effects are likely quite spatially specific around the saccade target <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Greenwood et al., 2017)</ref>, rather than representing an increase in attention to the entire scene <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Castelhano & Pereira, 2018</ref>).

text.text: Overall, our results extend our understanding of presaccadic attention, pushing into the context of dynamic, evolving, scenes for the first time, and show the characteristic change in localization accuracy across covert attention, presaccadic attention and overt attention conditions.

We do not claim that these results are particularly unexpected on their face, as one would expect saccade planning processes to be the same regardless of stimuli, but it remains necessary to test and validate our assumptions about how these systems behave in environments which more closely approximate the world outside the laboratory.

Future work here could investigate other well-established questions in this space, including whether the target of the impending saccade is represented in more detail and, if this is the case, whether it is represented as features or objects, although there are considerable challenges to doing this with natural video.

To assess whether differences in click error between the gaze-contingent video termination conditions were influenced by saccade latency, we fitted two linear mixed-effects models to the condition-level z-score data.
In both models, the dependent variable was the mean hazard-localization z-score for each participant in each auditory cue timing and gaze-contingent video termination condition.

Auditory cue timing and gaze-contingent video termination condition were entered as categorical fixed effects, mean post-cue saccade latency for first saccade towards video was entered as a continuous fixed effect, and participant was included as a random intercept.
The first model included only main effect of saccade latency, whereas the second model also included an interaction between saccade latency and gaze-contingent video termination condition.
Neither model showed a significant main effect of saccade latency or a significant interaction involving saccade latency.
Accordingly, these analyses are reported in the Supplementary Materials.

To examine whether differences in localization performance reflected more accurate saccade planning rather than differences in visual information use, we repeated the primary analyses using overt attention mean z-scores per unique level as the dependent variable.

This included a 3x3 repeated measures ANOVA across auditory cue timing and gaze contingent video termination condition including an interaction between the conditions, as well as a separate ANOVA restricted to the hazard-onset cue condition.
Overall, 1368 trials, accounting for 18.63% of all trials, were excluded according to the trial-level exclusion criteria.
